Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
I work hard at keeping busy with other things
repeatedly blame myself for what happened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

vignette: At seventy-eight, Clara Reyes had spent decades reconstructing a quiet life in Ohio, yet the ground beneath her feet still felt provisional. Thirty-eight years ago, while living in a coastal town in Guatemala, the night sky tore open with artillery. She remembered the acrid bite of burning tires and the heavy, wet scent of diesel as soldiers swept through her neighborhood. The military had come for her brother, and when he did not return, Clara was forced onto a crowded bus with nothing but the clothes on her back. She never saw him again, and the silence where his voice should have been settled into her chest like a stone. In the years that followed, the past did not arrive in words but as a sudden, overwhelming sensory intrusion. When the damp, earthy smell of a rainstorm or the faint whiff of diesel from a passing truck caught her off guard, her entire body would lock into a state of watchful alertness. The unspoken weight of those fragmented impressions would immediately sharpen her senses until she was scanning the room for exits, convinced that the danger she had fled could materialize at any moment. This constant state of high alert made it nearly impossible for her to focus on the catalog cards or the quiet pages of the reference section where she now worked. The longer she tried to process the daily demands of the library, the more her world shrank until she only felt secure within the familiar, sunlit periphery of her kitchen and the enclosed space of her marital bedroom. Because her baseline vigilance never settled and her circle of safe places remained tightly confined, she had learned to occupy every waking hour with meticulous routines. She would spend hours cross-referencing archives and meticulously reorganizing the local history stacks, forcing herself to stay constantly active because stillness left her too exposed to her own thoughts. Yet even as she worked, a quiet, relentless questioning took hold in her mind. She found herself cycling over the circumstances of that night, convinced that her own hesitation to leave the house sooner had somehow sealed her brother's fate, replaying her own perceived failures over and over until the guilt became suffocating. The exhausting effort to maintain this endless cycle of labor and self-accusation only kept her nervous system permanently wound, ensuring that her baseline vigilance never truly settled and her circle of safe places remained tightly confined. The constant mental exhaustion of scanning for threats gradually pulled the fragmented, wordless images back into sharp focus. The harder she tried to outrun her own thoughts by overworking or dissecting her past choices, the more vividly the unspoken scenes returned, each time carrying a fresh wave of profound remorse. For months, Clara had managed by burying herself in her husband's quiet support and her library duties, but recently the fatigue had become too heavy to carry alone. The realization that her own mind had become a place she could no longer inhabit finally broke her endurance. She scheduled her first appointment with a therapist, terrified that she was losing her husband to the ghost she could not outrun, yet desperately hoping to find a way to finally lay the heavy, unspoken grief to rest.
